newsitem.title: RUSSIA: This time, Russians believe the Kremlin on health.
newsitem.headline: This time, Russians believe the Kremlin on health.

text.p: Despite years of hearing lies from Kremlin about their ailing leaders, many Muscovites appear to believe the official version that President Boris Yeltsin is not facing any life-threatening illness.
"Everything has changed, and now they are telling the truth," said pensioner Nina Bondareva, 77. "Nothing is hidden. After all, everything is on television."
Government officials announced late Wednesday that Yeltsin, 65, was suffering from early signs of pneumonia just over two weeks after returning to the Kremlin following heart surgery.
His temperature is normal but he is taking antibiotics, the Kremlin said in a statement on Thursday.
The news halted a surge on the Russian stock market which had soared to record levels in recent days, and caused concern among foreign observers about the president's ability to lead.
But for average Muscovites who trudge the snow- and ice-covered streets under constant cover of gray winter clouds, a touch of pneumonia or flu sounds very believable.
"Everybody is sick these days in Moscow," said Dima Chernikov, 18, a university student. "I play soccer and in my team, 12 or 13 of my 20 teammates have fallen ill. It could happen to anybody."

For years, Soviet officials explained a leader's prolonged absence from the Kremlin as a cold or flu, hiding major health problems. Even as three leaders died in rapid succession in the mid 1980s, their health remained a Soviet state secret.
Yeltsin has not always been totally forthcoming about his ailments. After disappearing from public view following his re-election in June, his staff said he had suffered "colossal weariness."

But in September Yeltsin broke with tradition and announced he would undergo major heart surgery, which took place in November. This was followed by detailed media briefings, which helped boost the Kremlin's credibility.
"He is a human being after all," teacher Klara Ruskaya, 50, said on Thursday. "He has a right to be sick -- we have flu all over Moscow."
Some maintained traditional Russian scepticism however.
"First they said he had the flu, now they say it's the first signs of pneumonia. Only God knows what he really has," said Alexander Maksutov, 63, a postal worker.
The president's latest illness is prompting some to wonder if he is still able to run a country as vast and complicated as Russia.

"Under Russian law, if someone is sick for three months, they can be fired," said Rafael Mangushov, 47, assistant director of an insurance company. "Perhaps we are now arriving at that point. If he doesn't get better, then it raises the question of whether he can continue to lead."
Renat Akchurin, the doctor who led Yeltsin's November heart surgery, on Thursday reiterated the Kremlin line that the president is fit enough to rule.
"He is a completely normal and capable person; what's all this talk about? It's pure political speculation," he said.
